sections.title: 1. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
sections.overview: The SEC is the federal agency created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 with statutory authority over the U.S. securities markets. It administers and enforces the federal securities laws (1933 Act, 1934 Act, Trust Indenture Act of 1939, Investment Company Act of 1940, Investment Advisers Act of 1940, Sarbanes-Oxley, Dodd-Frank, JOBS Act) and oversees SROs, broker-dealers, investment advisers, transfer agents, clearing agencies, and registered investment companies.
key_concepts: Created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 — not an SRO; it is a federal regulator with civil enforcement authority (criminal matters are referred to the DOJ).
Five Commissioners, appointed by the President with Senate confirmation, serving staggered 5-year terms; no more than 3 may be from the same political party. The President designates one as Chair.
Five operating divisions: Corporation Finance, Trading and Markets, Investment Management, Enforcement, and Economic and Risk Analysis.

Authority includes registering securities offerings (1933 Act), registering and overseeing broker-dealers and SROs (1934 Act), approving SRO rules, granting/denying registrations, and issuing no-action letters and interpretive guidance.
SEC reviews disciplinary actions of SROs and rule filings; SRO rules become effective only upon SEC approval (or filing under self-effectuating categories).
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(39) — defines 'statutory disqualification,' the conditions under which a person is barred from association with an SRO member (includes specified felony/securities-related misdemeanor convictions within 10 years, SEC/SRO bars, willful false statements on registration forms, and certain injunctions).
17 CFR 240.17f-2 — SEC fingerprinting rule for securities-industry personnel; submission via an authorized SRO/agency.
mnemonics: SEC Commissioners: '5 / 5 / 3' — 5 Commissioners, 5-year staggered terms, no more than 3 from one party.
Divisions — 'CITE-E': Corp Finance, Investment Management, Trading & Markets, Enforcement, Economic & Risk Analysis.

sections.title: 2. U.S. Treasury Branches with Securities-Related Authority
sections.overview: Several bureaus inside the Department of the Treasury exercise authority that touches the securities industry, particularly in the areas of banking, AML, and tax. The SIE expects candidates to know which Treasury bureau performs which function.
key_concepts: OCC (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) — charters, regulates, and supervises all national banks and federal savings associations; oversees bank securities activities conducted under bank exceptions.

FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) — administers the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and AML rules; receives Currency Transaction Reports (CTRs over $10,000) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs); designated as the U.S. Financial Intelligence Unit under the USA PATRIOT Act.
IRS (Internal Revenue Service) — administers the Internal Revenue Code; oversees retirement-account tax rules, cost-basis reporting, and information returns (1099, 5498, etc.).
These bureaus are not SROs and do not enforce FINRA rules, but BSA/AML compliance and tax-reporting obligations are integral to BD operations.
mnemonics: Treasury trio for the SIE: 'OFI' — OCC (banks), FinCEN (AML), IRS (tax).

sections.title: 3. SIPC vs. FDIC — Customer Protection Coverage
sections.overview: SIPC (Securities Investor Protection Corporation) protects customers of failed broker-dealers; FDIC (Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation) protects depositors of failed insured banks. Both are limited to defined coverage amounts and do NOT protect against investment losses from market movement.
key_concepts: SIPC was created by the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 (SIPA); membership is mandatory for nearly all registered U.S. broker-dealers.

SIPC coverage: up to $500,000 per separate customer (per separate capacity), of which a maximum of $250,000 may be cash. Securities held in 'street name' are protected; commodities futures, fixed annuities, and unregistered investment contracts are NOT covered.
Separate capacities (each gets its own limit): individual, joint, IRA, Roth IRA, custodian (UTMA/UGMA), corporate, trust, etc.
If a BD fails, SIPC may petition a court to appoint a trustee to liquidate the firm; customer claims have priority over general creditors.

FDIC coverage: $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. Covers deposit products (checking, savings, CDs, MMDA) — NOT securities, mutual funds, or annuities, even if purchased at a bank.
Bank-sweep money market deposit accounts are FDIC-insured; money market mutual funds in a brokerage account are SIPC-protected but not FDIC-insured.
formulas: SIPC max per separate capacity = $500,000 total securities + cash, with cash sub-limit = $250,000
FDIC max = $250,000 per depositor / per insured bank / per ownership category
mnemonics: FDIC: '2.5 per category, per bank, per depositor.'
SIPC ≠ insurance against losing money — it's protection against the BD's failure.

sections.title: 4. State Administrators and NASAA
sections.overview: State (or 'blue-sky') securities regulation operates in parallel with federal regulation. State administrators register securities, broker-dealers, agents (registered reps), and investment adviser representatives under the Uniform Securities Act, and they coordinate through the North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA).
key_concepts: Blue-sky laws — state securities statutes; typically modeled on the Uniform Securities Act (1956/2002).
Three-pronged state registration: (1) the security, (2) the broker-dealer/investment adviser firm, (3) the agent / IAR.

NSMIA (1996) preempted state registration of 'covered securities' (e.g., NYSE/Nasdaq-listed securities, investment company shares) but left states authority over fraud enforcement and notice-filing fees.
State administrators may deny, suspend, or revoke a registration; sanctions can include statutory disqualification from FINRA.
NASAA — not a regulator itself; an association of state administrators that drafts model rules and the Series 63/65/66 exams.
Form U4 / Form U10 are filed via FINRA's CRD system, which interfaces with state regulators.
mnemonics: Three to register at the state level: 'Security – Firm – Agent.'

sections.title: 5. FINRA — Scope and Authority
sections.overview: FINRA (Financial Industry Regulatory Authority) is the largest non-governmental SRO for U.S. broker-dealers. It was formed in 2007 by the consolidation of NASD with the member regulation, enforcement, and arbitration functions of the NYSE. FINRA writes rules subject to SEC approval, examines members, enforces its rules and the federal securities laws against members, and operates the BrokerCheck system and the dispute-resolution forum.
key_concepts: Definition of 'member' — Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §3(a)(3)(B): a broker or dealer who agrees to be regulated by the association.
FINRA jurisdiction covers member firms and their associated persons; FINRA does not directly regulate issuers, investors, or non-member banks.
FINRA Code of Procedure (Rule 9000 series) — handles disciplinary proceedings (complaints, hearings, sanctions, appeals).

FINRA Code of Arbitration (Rule 12000/13000) — mandatory forum for disputes between members, between members and associated persons, and between members and customers (when the customer signs an arbitration agreement or files a claim).
Sanctions FINRA may impose: censure, fine, suspension, bar (permanent), expulsion of the firm, restitution.
BrokerCheck — public disclosure tool (Rule 8312) showing registration and disciplinary history of firms and registered persons.
Customer education: members must annually furnish customers the FINRA BrokerCheck hotline number, website, and brochure availability (Rule 2267).
rules: Rule 1122 — Prohibits filing of misleading membership/registration information; failure to correct is itself a violation.

Rule 1240 — Continuing Education: Regulatory Element (annually, by Dec. 31, per registration category) and Firm Element (annual needs analysis and written training plan for covered registered persons). Failure to complete Regulatory Element renders registration inactive; two consecutive years of inactivity terminates the registration.
Rule 2060 — Prohibits use of customer/security-ownership information obtained in a fiduciary capacity (e.g., as transfer agent or paying agent) to solicit business.
Rule 2263 — Arbitration disclosure must be provided when an associated person signs or acknowledges Form U4 (disclosing waiver of jury trial, limited discovery, finality of awards, etc.).
Rule 2267 — Annual delivery of FINRA BrokerCheck information to customers.
Rule 2310(c) — Non-cash compensation limits for direct participation programs.
Rule 2320(g)(4) — Non-cash compensation limits for variable contracts.
Rule 2341(l)(5) — Non-cash compensation limits for investment company securities.

Rule 3110(e) — Background investigation of registration applicants; member must verify the accuracy and completeness of the information on Form U4, including a search of public records, within 30 calendar days of filing.

Rule 3220 — 'Gifts Rule': gifts or gratuities to employees of others related to the recipient's business are limited to $300 per person, per year; written employment-agreement exception requires prior written consent of the recipient's employer.
Rule 3270 — Outside business activities of registered persons: prior written notice to the member required before engaging.
Rule 3280 — Private securities transactions ('selling away'): prior written notice and, if compensation is received, prior written approval of the member; firm must record on its books if approved.
Rule 4513 — Records of written customer complaints (retain at each OSJ for at least 4 years).
Rule 4330 — Customer-securities lending; permission and disclosures required for firms borrowing from customers (fully paid / excess-margin securities).

Rule 4530 — Reporting obligations of members: must report to FINRA specified events (criminal charges/convictions, customer complaints, regulatory actions, etc.); statistical/summary complaint reporting quarterly; certain events within 30 days.
Rule 5110(h) — Non-cash compensation in connection with public offerings.
Rule 8312 — BrokerCheck disclosure of information by FINRA.
formulas: FINRA Rule 3220 gift cap = $300 per individual per year
Rule 4530 reporting deadline for specified events = within 30 calendar days of knowledge
Rule 3110(e) background-check completion = within 30 calendar days of Form U4 filing
mnemonics: FINRA sanctions ladder — 'CFSBE': Censure, Fine, Suspension, Bar, Expulsion.
Reportable conduct deadlines: 'Thirty for the firm, Thirty for the rep' — 30 days under Rule 4530 / Form U4 amendments.
Selling-away vs. moonlighting: 'Securities = approval (3280); Other = notice (3270).'

sections.title: 6. MSRB and the Exchanges
sections.overview: The MSRB (Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board) writes rules governing municipal securities dealers, brokers, and municipal advisors, but it does NOT examine or enforce. The national securities exchanges (NYSE, Nasdaq, CBOE) are SROs that operate marketplaces and write rules governing their members.
key_concepts: MSRB created by the Securities Acts Amendments of 1975; SEC-overseen, self-regulatory, but does NOT enforce its own rules.
MSRB rules are enforced by: FINRA (for securities firms), the SEC, the OCC (national banks), the Federal Reserve (state member banks), and the FDIC (insured state non-member banks).

Exchanges (Securities Exchange Act §3(a)(1)) — organizations that bring together purchasers and sellers; must register with the SEC as national securities exchanges. Examples: NYSE, Nasdaq Stock Market, Cboe BZX, NYSE Arca.
CBOE (Cboe Options Exchange) writes options-trading rules; FINRA enforces options rules at non-Cboe member firms.
Member definitions: SEA §3(a)(3)(A) (exchange member) and §3(a)(3)(B) (association member).
rules: MSRB Rule G-2 — Standards of professional qualification; persons engaging in municipal securities activities must be qualified per MSRB rules.
MSRB Rule G-3 — Classification of municipal securities representatives (Series 52) and principals (Series 53); CE requirements parallel to FINRA's (Regulatory and Firm Element).
MSRB Rule G-7 — Information concerning associated persons (analog to Form U4 disclosures for muni personnel).
MSRB Rule G-10 — Annual investor-education notice and disclosure to customers regarding MSRB website, investor brochure, and complaint procedures.

MSRB Rule G-20 — Gifts, gratuities, non-cash compensation, and expenses of issuance — the muni equivalent of FINRA Rule 3220; $100 per person per year limit on gifts in relation to municipal securities/advisory business.

MSRB Rule G-37 — Political contributions and prohibitions on municipal securities business: a dealer is banned from engaging in municipal securities business with an issuer for two years if the dealer or a 'municipal finance professional' makes a non-de-minimis contribution to an issuer official with influence over the award of business. De minimis: contributions of $250 or less per election to an official for whom the MFP is entitled to vote do not trigger the ban; quarterly Form G-37 disclosure required.
Cboe Rule 7.10 — Disciplinary rules / sanctions for exchange members (used as authority for CBOE enforcement actions).
formulas: MSRB G-20 gift cap = $100 per individual per year (vs. FINRA $300)
MSRB G-37 de minimis contribution = $250 per election, per official the MFP can vote for; ban for violations = 2 years from the issuer
mnemonics: MSRB 'writes but doesn't fight' — it writes rules but does not examine/enforce.
G-37 = 'Two-50, Two-year ban' — $250 de minimis / 2-year MFAB prohibition.

sections.title: 7. Record-Retention Requirements
sections.overview: SEC Rules 17a-3 (records to be made) and 17a-4 (records to be preserved) under the Exchange Act establish the federal record-keeping framework for broker-dealers. Retention periods vary by document type; certain core organizational records must be kept for the life of the firm.
key_concepts: SEA Rule 17a-3 — specifies which records a BD must create (blotters, ledgers, order tickets, trade confirmations, account records, etc.).
SEA Rule 17a-4 — specifies how long each record must be preserved and the storage format (immediate accessibility for a specified period, then off-site).
Life-of-firm records — partnership articles, articles of incorporation, charter, minute books, stock certificate books.
6-year records — blotters, general ledgers, stock records (securities position records), customer account ledgers (often kept 6 years after account closed).

3-year records — most other records, including order tickets, trade confirmations, customer correspondence, communications with the public, advertising, employment applications (3 years after termination), Forms U4 (after termination), trial balances, and FOCUS reports. Communications typically 3 years, the first 2 years in an easily accessible place.

Rule 17a-4(f) was amended in 2023 (SEC Release No. 34-96034) to permit broker-dealers to use an 'audit-trail alternative' to the legacy WORM (write-once-read-many) electronic storage requirement; the underlying retention periods are unchanged for SIE purposes.
FINRA Rule 4513 — written customer complaints retained at the OSJ for at least 4 years.
Audit-trail reporting — the Consolidated Audit Trail (CAT) replaced OATS effective September 1, 2021; CAT captures the full lifecycle of an order across markets.
rules: 17 CFR 240.17a-3 — books and records to be made.
17 CFR 240.17a-4 — preservation of records; 17a-4(f) audit-trail/electronic storage requirements.
FINRA Rule 4513 — customer complaint records (4 years at OSJ).
FINRA Rule 4530 — interfaces with retention by setting reporting deadlines for specified events.
formulas: Common retention periods (SEA 17a-4): Lifetime → org/charter docs; 6 years → blotters, GL, stock record, customer account ledgers; 3 years → most other records (order tickets, confirms, correspondence, ads, U4/U5 after termination)
FINRA Rule 4513 customer complaint records = 4 years at the OSJ
mnemonics: Retention ladder — 'Life / 6 / 4 / 3': Life-of-firm (charter); 6 yrs (blotters, ledgers, stock record); 4 yrs (complaints – Rule 4513); 3 yrs (everything else / communications).
OATS → CAT: 'Old Audit Trail System' was replaced by the 'Consolidated Audit Trail' on 9/1/2021.
WORM is no longer the only option — audit-trail alternative permitted under amended 17a-4(f).
